name: Fusidic acid/betamethasone (topical)
className: Potent topical corticosteroid (group III) with antibiotic

formulations.label: Cream
formulations.note: Contains cetostearyl alcohol (local skin reactions) and chlorocresol (allergic reactions).

src.q: contains Fusidic acid Ph.Eur.2% and Betamethasone 0.1% (as the valerate ester Ph.Eur)
Cetostearyl alcohol may cause local skin reactions (e.g. contact dermatitis) and chlorocresol may cause allergic reactions.

bnf.note: BNF/BNFC is only available in the UK; not accessed.

items.t: Eczematous dermatoses (atopic, infantile, discoid, stasis, contact and seborrhoeic eczema) when secondary bacterial infection is confirmed or suspected.

src.q: indicated for the treatment of eczematous dermatoses including atopic eczema, infantile eczema, discoid eczema, stasis eczema, contact eczema and seborrhoeic eczema when secondary bacterial infection is confirmed or suspected

items.t: Potent steroid: labelled as a strong steroid (MHRA potency labelling for topical steroids).

src.q: The label will state strong steroid.
Betamethasone is classed as a potent corticosteroid.

items.t: Apply a small quantity twice daily until a satisfactory response. A single course should not normally exceed 2 weeks. In more resistant lesions, polythene occlusion (usually overnight) can increase the effect.

src.q: A small quantity should be applied to the affected area twice daily until a satisfactory response is obtained.
A single treatment course should not normally exceed 2 weeks.
Overnight occlusion is usually adequate.

items.t: Limit treatment to no more than 14 days at a time (reduces resistance and the risk of masking resistant infection).

src.q: Limiting therapy with topical fusidic acid and betamethasone valerate to no more than 14 days at a time will minimise the risk of developing resistance.

items.t: Use with care in children (more susceptible to HPA-axis suppression and Cushing's syndrome): avoid large amounts, occlusion and prolonged treatment. Safety profile is otherwise similar to adults.

src.q: Fucibet® should be used with care in children as paediatric patients may demonstrate greater susceptibility to topical corticosteroids-induced HPA axis suppression and Cushing's syndrome than adult patients.
Avoid large amounts, occlusion and prolonged treatment
The observed safety profile is similar in children and adults

items.t: Hypersensitivity to fusidic acid (sodium fusidate), betamethasone valerate or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to fusidic acid/sodium fusidate, betamethasone valerate or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Systemic fungal infections; primary skin infections caused by fungi, viruses or bacteria that are untreated or uncontrolled; untreated or uncontrolled skin tuberculosis or syphilis; perioral dermatitis; rosacea.

src.q: Systemic fungal infections. Primary skin infections caused by fungi, virus or bacteria, either untreated or uncontrolled by appropriate treatment
Skin manifestations in relation to tuberculosis or syphilis, either untreated or uncontrolled by appropriate therapy. Perioral dermatitis and rosacea.

items.t: Avoid long-term continuous use; prolonged use may cause skin atrophy. Consider systemic absorption depending on the site (HPA-axis suppression possible).

src.q: Long-term continuous topical therapy with Fucibet® should be avoided.
prolonged topical use of Fucibet® may cause skin atrophy
Reversible hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis suppression may occur following systemic absorption of topical corticosteroids.

items.t: Use with care near the eyes and avoid getting it into the eyes. Blurred vision or other visual disturbance: consider referral to an ophthalmologist.

src.q: should be used with care near the eyes. Avoid getting Fucibet® into the eyes
the patient should be considered for referral to an ophthalmologist for evaluation of possible causes

items.t: Steroid may increase susceptibility to infection, worsen existing infection or activate latent infection. Fusidic acid resistance has been reported. Switch to systemic treatment if infection is not controlled.

src.q: may be associated with increased susceptibility to infection, aggravation of existing infection, and activation of latent infection
It is advised to switch to systemic treatment if infection cannot be controlled with topical treatment

items.t: Topical steroid withdrawal: long-term use can cause rebound flares after stopping (intense redness, stinging, burning spreading beyond the treated area), more likely on the face and flexures. MHRA: risk is higher with prolonged use of moderate or stronger steroids (generally 6 months or more), particularly for eczema.

src.q: Long term use of topical steroids can result in the development of rebound flares after stopping treatment (topical steroid withdrawal syndrome).
adverse reactions have been reported following long-term (generally 6 months or more) use of moderate or stronger potency topical steroids, particularly when used for eczema treatment

items.t: Fire hazard: fabric in contact with the cream burns more easily; patients must not smoke or go near naked flames.

src.q: Instruct patients not to smoke or go near naked flames - risk of severe burns.

items.t: No interaction studies; interactions with systemic medicines are considered minimal.

src.q: Interactions with systemically administered medicinal products are considered minimal.

renal.note: The UK SmPC gives no renal advice.

hepatic.note: The UK SmPC gives no hepatic advice.

items.t: Should not be used in pregnancy unless clearly necessary: little or no data for topical betamethasone valerate in pregnant women; animal studies showed reproductive toxicity.

src.q: Fucibet® should not be used during pregnancy unless clearly necessary.
There are no or limited amount of data from the use of topical betamethasone valerate in pregnant women.
Studies in animals have shown reproductive toxicity/foetal abnormalities

items.t: BUMPS (topical corticosteroids as a class; betamethasone is not named in the leaflet): can be used in pregnancy.

src.q: Topical corticosteroids can be used in pregnancy.

items.t: Can be used during breastfeeding, but do not apply to the breasts (risk of the infant swallowing it).

src.q: can be used during breast-feeding but should not be applied on the breasts to avoid accidental ingestion by the infant

items.t: SPS: betamethasone on the skin can be used during breastfeeding (high potency); no extra risk from antimicrobial combinations. Large areas for long periods may need infant monitoring of feeding, growth and weight.

src.q: When applied to the skin, or for rectal, intranasal, ophthalmic use, or for use in the ear, betamethasone can be used during breastfeeding.
Betamethasone is considered high potency when applied as a cream or ointment. There are no additional risks when combination products containing antimicrobials or salicylic acid are used.

items.t: No clinical studies on fertility.

src.q: There are no clinical studies with Fucibet® regarding fertility

items.t: No common effects listed. Most frequently reported: itching. Uncommon: contact dermatitis, worsening eczema, burning, dry skin, application-site pain or irritation.

src.q: The most frequently reported adverse reaction during treatment is pruritus.
Dermatitis contact Eczema (condition aggravated) Skin burning sensation Pruritus Dry skin

items.t: Hypersensitivity (uncommon).

src.q: Immune system disorders Uncommon: (≥1/1,000 and <1/100) Hypersensitivity

items.t: Adrenal suppression with prolonged use; raised intra-ocular pressure, glaucoma or cataract if used near the eyes. Large amounts for more than 3 weeks can cause Cushing's syndrome and adrenocortical insufficiency.

src.q: Systemic undesirable class effects of corticosteroids like betamethasone valerate include adrenal suppression especially during prolonged topical administration
Raised intra-ocular pressure, glaucoma or cataract may also occur after topical use of corticosteroids near the eyes
Cushing's syndrome and adrenocortical insufficiency may develop following topical application of corticosteroids in large amounts and for more than three weeks.

items.t: MHRA: adrenal suppression (low blood pressure, dizziness, fainting) is life-threatening and needs urgent treatment; stopping suddenly is dangerous if adrenal suppression is present.

src.q: This is a serious, life-threatening condition that needs urgent treatment.
Stopping the topical steroid suddenly is dangerous if there is adrenal suppression

items.t: Topical steroid withdrawal reactions after stopping: spreading redness, burning or stinging, itch, peeling, oozing pustules.

src.q: Withdrawal reactions - redness of the skin which may extend to areas beyond the initial affected area, burning or stinging sensation, itch, skin peeling, oozing pustules

items.t: Switch to systemic treatment if infection is not controlled; do not exceed a 2-week course without review.

src.q: It is advised to switch to systemic treatment if infection cannot be controlled with topical treatment
A single treatment course should not normally exceed 2 weeks.

items.t: Thinned skin can be hard to see in brown or black skin, so careful monitoring is needed; be vigilant for withdrawal reactions.

src.q: This can be very difficult to see in brown or black skin, therefore careful monitoring is required.
be vigilant for the signs and symptoms of topical steroid withdrawal reactions

items.t: For use on the skin only. Apply a small quantity; keep away from the eyes.

src.q: Method of administration Cutaneous use
Avoid getting Fucibet® into the eyes

items.t: Explain how much to apply, how often, where, and when to stop; if using steroids of different strengths on different areas, use the right one for each area.

src.q: when prescribing or dispensing topical steroids, advise on the amount of product to apply, how often, where to apply it and when to stop treatment
if using more than one topical steroid on different body areas, ensure you are using the correct strength for the area of the body concerned

items.t: If the skin worsens within 2 weeks of stopping, do not restart without consulting the doctor (unless already advised).

src.q: if your skin worsens within 2 weeks of stopping a topical corticosteroid, do not start treatment again without consulting your doctor

items.t: Do not smoke or go near naked flames: clothing, bedding and dressings with cream on them burn more easily.

src.q: Fabric (clothing, bedding, dressings etc) that has been in contact with this product burns more easily and is a serious fire hazard.
